text: New England Regional SAF Hub in June 2025 to unite industries and sectors for the purpose of developing strategies, partnerships, and policy frameworks to accelerate SAF adoption (Massport 2025a). The working group for this effort released a report Recommendations to the Governor on Accelerating the Adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuels in Massachusetts and New England, which established a plan to incentivize the use of SAF as well as develop a regional SAF industry (Massport 2025a). As a part of this effort, Massport funded the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) to prepare a SAF study. This study evaluated the potential SAF production in New England and a logistics assessment for using SAF in the region regardless of where it is produced. A resource assessment was completed to determine SAF feedstock availability within a 50- and 100-mile radius of 10 New England airports selected by Massport. These airports include BOS, Laurence G. Hanscom Field (BED), and Worcester Regional Airport (ORH), all owned by Massport, as well as Bradley International Airport (BDL), Martha’s Vineyard Airport (MVY), Portland International Jetport (PWM), Portsmouth International Airport at Pease (PSM), Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport (PVD), Manchester-Boston Regional Airport (MHT), and Westfield-Barnes Regional Airport (BAF). The biomass resource assessment evaluated vegetable and waste oils, wet organic waste, municipal solid waste (MSW), and lignocellulosic biomass (woody biomass and crop residues). Results indicate that MSW and food waste are the most abundant resources within both 50- and 100-mile radii, reflecting the airports’ locations in densely populated urban areas. Some overlap in resource availability occurs due to the proximity of the airports. Vegetable oils and related byproducts are not locally available but could be sourced from other regions, while sources of manure (livestock operations) were not identified near the selected airports. A techno-economic analysis (TEA) was conducted to evaluate the feasibility of producing SAF from various biomass feedstocks. This analysis utilized data derived from a comprehensive resource assessment of potential feedstocks available within a specific region. Boston. The airports’ infrastructure and accessibility were deemed conducive to the establishment of a SAF production facility. Exceptions were made for woody biomass, where PWM was selected as the TEA location due to its strategic proximity to Maine’s robust and well- established wood industry and its existing infrastructure for handling and transporting wood products. This site selection optimized access to feedstock and facilitated the assessment of relevant processing pathways. The analysis of bioenergy production potentials around ten New England airports reveal strong opportunities for localized renewable fuel generation. BDL and BAF airports show the highest total potentials—519 and 436 MMgge/yr3, respectively—while Massachusetts airports dominate overall.
